HIST 101 • Chapter 3 • Lecture 4

Could the King Just Do Whatever He Wanted?

Empire, consent, and English rights in the 1680s

Image description: Textbook image 3.7, A London Coffeehouse, shows an eighteenth-century coffeehouse where merchants and readers meet. The image is used as atmosphere for the world of Atlantic commerce, political debate, and imperial administration.

Cold-open guidance: begin with the cancellation scenario. Ask whether students would be angrier about a tax itself or about being taxed by a government in which they had no meaningful voice. That question drives the entire lecture.

Your Government Is Cancelled

The central government replaces your elected leaders.

It changes land rules, collects taxes, and says your old charter no longer protects you.

Is the problem the policy - or the power to impose it?

One-Minute Choice

A high tax
approved by your own elected representatives
A lower tax
imposed by officials you did not choose

Which would anger you more?

Mercantilism Was a Power Theory

wealth→ shipping→ navy→ empire
Colonies should supply raw materials and buy the mother country's goods.

Not simply greed - a seventeenth-century theory of national strength.

Salem: Why Fear Becomes Believable

Do not begin with: “They were just superstitious.”

The better question is why accusations exploded in Massachusetts in 1692.

The witch crisis began in Samuel Parris's household, then spread through Salem Village and Essex County.

So, Could the King Do Whatever He Wanted?

No. The Glorious Revolution rejected arbitrary monarchy and reaffirmed English liberties.
But also no independence. The result was stronger imperial oversight inside constitutional limits.

The Paradox to Keep

Colonial self-government and imperial power
grew together.

That tension will not disappear.

Next Question

Colonists enter the eighteenth century proud of being British
and proud of their English liberties.

What happens when those loyalties later collide?

1689 Did Not Play Out the Same Everywhere

ColonyLocal meaning of revolution
BostonAndros overthrown and old governments restored, though Massachusetts later receives a changed charter.
New YorkLeislerian and Anti-Leislerian factions battle over authority, ethnicity, religion, and loyalty.
MarylandProtestants overthrow Catholic proprietary government and end the earlier toleration experiment.

The Glorious Revolution became colonial politics as soon as it crossed the Atlantic.

The Financial Revolution

public debt→ Bank of England→ new taxes→ war power
Constitutional government did not make Britain weak. It helped make the British state more capable.

Religious Fear in an Atlantic World

  • James II was Catholic
  • Louis XIV persecuted Huguenots
  • New England feared Catholic and Native enemies
  • Protestant identity became imperial glue
Anti-Catholic fear helped connect English politics, empire, and colonial anxiety.

1 / 32
×
mercantilism

A seventeenth-century theory that national power depended on national wealth and that colonies should be organized to strengthen the mother country's trade, shipping, revenue, and military capacity.

×
Navigation Acts

English laws passed between 1651 and 1673 that required much colonial trade to move through English ships and markets, especially important commodities such as tobacco and sugar.

×
Dominion of New England

A centralized royal administration created under James II that combined colonies north of Pennsylvania under Governor Edmund Andros and replaced much of the older charter-based local government.

×
Edmund Andros

Royal governor of the Dominion of New England. He became the human face of imperial centralization, especially because he governed without elected assemblies and enforced trade and land policies more aggressively.

×
Glorious Revolution

The 1688-1689 overthrow of James II and installation of William and Mary. It limited arbitrary monarchy, reaffirmed Parliament's control over taxation and legislation, and reshaped colonial expectations about English rights.

×
English rights

A language of legitimate government that linked taxation, property, law, and representation to the rights colonists believed they possessed as English subjects inside the empire.
